ety.text: Inherited from Middle English hauk, hauke, hawke, havek, from Old English hafoc, from Proto-West Germanic *habuk, from Proto-Germanic *habukaz, controversially derived from Proto-Indo-European *kopuǵos, perhaps ultimately derived from *kap- (“seize”).
Uncertain; perhaps from Middle English hache (“battle-axe”), or from a variant use of the above, for this compare with Russian со́кол (sókol, “falcon, but also a hawk (plaster's tool), mortarboard”).
Probably imitative, like hock (“cough”), hack (“cough”), although see the latter entry for more.

senses.d: A diurnal predatory bird of the family Accipitridae, smaller than an eagle.
ex: It is illegal to hunt hawks or other raptors in many parts of the world.

He made his hawke to fly,
With hogeous showte and cry.

senses.d: Any diurnal predatory terrestrial bird of similar size and appearance to the accipitrid hawks, such as a falcon.
Any of various species of dragonfly of the genera Apocordulia and Austrocordulia, endemic to Australia.
An advocate of aggressive political positions and actions.
ex: President Donald Trump has spent years playing the role of a China hawk.

senses.d: An uncooperative or purely selfish participant in an exchange or game, especially when untrusting, acquisitive or treacherous. Refers specifically to the prisoner's dilemma, a.k.a. the Hawk-Dove game.

ex: I wanna learn by Ruby's birthday party." Pride turned up his collar against the hawk blowing from the river."

To hawke, or els to hunt
From the auter to the funt
He rode astride while hawking; she falconed in the ladylike position of sidesaddle.

senses.d: To make an attack while on the wing; to soar and strike like a hawk.
ex: A falcon, towering in her pride of place, / Was by a mousing owl hawked at and killed.

senses.d: A plasterer's tool, made of a flat surface with a handle below, used to hold an amount of plaster prior to application to the wall or ceiling being worked on: a mortarboard.
To sell; to offer for sale by outcry in the street; to carry (merchandise) about from place to place for sale; to peddle.
ex: The vendors were hawking their wares from little tables lining either side of the market square.
His works were hawked in every street.

senses.d: A noisy effort to force up phlegm from the throat.
ex: The man gave a rattling hawk in his throat and spat directly between Bond and Leiter.

senses.d: To expectorate, to cough up (something, such as mucus) from one's throat; to produce (something) by coughing or clearing one's throat.
ex: [I]s a trobled with the cough a the Lunges ſtill? does he hawke anights ſtill?

senses.d: To try to cough up something from one's throat; to clear the throat loudly; to cough heavily, especially causing uvular frication.
ex: Grandpa sat on the front porch, hawking and wheezing, as he packed his pipe with cheap tobacco.

grp.label: to attempt to cough up, to clear the throat

ety.text: Inherited from Old French (h)ostur, from Late Latin auceptor, from accipiter.
Inherited from Late Latin falcō, probably of Germanic origin.
Of Germanic origin, from Proto-Germanic *sparwaraz (“sparrow-hawk”), from *sparwô (“sparrow”) + *arô (“eagle”). Compare French épervier. Cognate with sparrow.
From Old Spanish aztor, adtor, from Vulgar Latin *acceptor, replacement of Latin accipiter. For the simplification of the cluster, compare rezar from recitāre and plazo from placitum.
Probably from a derivative of Gothic *𐌲𐌰𐌱𐌹𐌻𐌰 (*gabila), which would be related to Proto-West Germanic *gabulu (“fork”); compare Portuguese gavião and Old High German gabila, gabala.

Inherited from Middle French faulcon, from Old French falcun (“falcon”), from Late Latin falcōnem, accusative form of falcō (“falcon”), probably of Germanic origin.
